openingProblem.problem: In 1983 US-Soviet relations reached their lowest point in years. By the end of 1991 the Soviet Union no longer existed. What ended the Cold War so quickly and so peacefully?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: who or what ended the Cold War?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Confrontation: the 'Second Cold War', 1979–1985
chunks.body:
By 1980 détente was dead. After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979, President Carter withdrew the SALT II treaty from the Senate, boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics and banned grain sales to the USSR. Two weeks before the invasion NATO had already decided to install 108 Pershing II and 464 Cruise missiles in Western Europe, its answer to new Soviet SS20 medium-range missiles. A new arms race seemed to be gathering speed.

**Ronald Reagan**, President from January 1981, set out to restore American strength. He modernised US nuclear and conventional forces and backed anti-Communist forces abroad. When the Polish regime declared martial law against the Solidarity movement in December 1981, he imposed further sanctions on Moscow. In 1983 he called the Soviet Union an "evil empire" and announced the **Strategic Defense Initiative** (SDI, "Star Wars"), a plan for missile defence that Soviet leaders found deeply threatening. In 1985 US defence spending rose by 6 per cent, an unprecedented peacetime increase.

The low point came in the autumn of 1983. The Soviets shot down a Korean airliner, KAL 007; NATO began deploying its new missiles; and Soviet negotiators walked out of the arms talks in Geneva. In Western Europe the missiles revived the peace movement: in October 1983 former Chancellor Willy Brandt urged 300,000 people in Bonn to reject them.

How dangerous was this "Second Cold War"? Tony Judt warns against exaggerating it. Neither side actually intended nuclear war, and much of Reagan's belligerence was rhetoric for a domestic audience; the same president was proposing nuclear arms reductions. But the danger of misunderstanding was real, because each side's leaders believed the other might be planning a pre-emptive strike. In the short run, Judt argues, Reagan's hard line, and SDI in particular, made the ageing Soviet leadership "even less disposed to compromise".

This mattered because confrontation raised the cost of the Cold War for a Soviet system already under strain, which meant that when a new Soviet leader came to power, ending the arms race became an urgent priority.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Afghanistan and the missile deployments ended détente.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: NATO's missile decision came before the invasion.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Reagan rearmed and used hostile rhetoric.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Judt says much of it was rhetoric for a domestic audience.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Confrontation hardened the Soviet leadership in the short run.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It also raised the cost of the arms race for the USSR.

chunks.title: A system under strain: economy, arms and Afghanistan
chunks.body:
Why could the Soviet Union not keep up? Part of the answer was the sheer burden of the arms race. The USSR had built a military machine that defeated Hitler, occupied half of Europe and matched the West weapon for weapon for forty years, but at a terrible price. At their peak, Judt writes, between 30 and 40 per cent of Soviet resources went to the military, four to five times the American share. Many Soviet experts already knew that the country could not carry this burden for ever.

The war in Afghanistan made things worse. Judt calls it "a catastrophe for the Soviet Union": a decade-long war of attrition against guerrillas armed and financed from abroad, and an extended international humiliation. It also changed what the Soviet leadership thought possible. As the Politburo member Yegor Ligachev later admitted, after Afghanistan "there could no longer be any question of applying force in Eastern Europe".

Did Reagan's arms build-up therefore bankrupt the Soviet Union? Judt rejects this as too simple. The American build-up "would come to be seen as the cunningly crafted lever that bankrupted and ultimately broke the Soviet system. This, however, is not quite accurate." The USSR could ill afford the arms race, but "bankruptcy alone would not have brought Communism to its knees". Neither Afghanistan nor the arms race would by themselves have caused collapse: Brezhnev's "era of stagnation", sustained by fear, inertia and self-interest, might have lasted indefinitely.

Ideological challenges and dissent also weakened the system. In Poland the independent trade union **Solidarity**, formed in August 1980, survived martial law underground with support from Western labour organisations and émigré groups. Judt notes that Solidarity was largely financed from the US.

This mattered because economic strain, a failing war and growing dissent created the conditions for change, which meant that the decisive question was how a Soviet leader would respond to them.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Judt says bankruptcy alone would not have brought collapse.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The war alone would not have caused collapse.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Dissent and Solidarity challenged Communist legitimacy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Martial law drove Solidarity underground in 1981.

chunks.title: Reconciliation: Gorbachev and Reagan, 1985–1988
chunks.body:
In March 1985 **Mikhail Gorbachev** became General Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party. Within a month he had halted Soviet missile deployments and offered negotiations on nuclear forces, starting with a proposal to halve the two strategic arsenals. Reagan now had a negotiating partner.

A series of summits followed. At Geneva, the first of five meetings, the two leaders established a working relationship. At **Reykjavik** in October 1986 they discussed abolishing all nuclear weapons; they failed to agree, but laid the basis for later success. In December 1987 they signed the **Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty**, which eliminated an entire class of missiles. By endorsing Reagan's earlier "zero option", Judt argues, it amounted to Soviet acceptance that a nuclear war in Europe was unwinnable. Gorbachev also pulled the Red Army out of Afghanistan, the "bleeding wound" as he called it: withdrawal began in May 1988 and the last troops left on 15 February 1989.

Why did Gorbachev make these concessions? Seen from Washington they looked like a victory for Reagan. But Judt stresses that Gorbachev's priorities were domestic: a calmer international environment bought him time and support for his reforms of **perestroika** (restructuring) and **glasnost** (openness). In October 1986 he declared that "ideology" was not an appropriate basis for foreign policy. He also thought of himself as a European statesman, speaking of a "European home" in which each apartment could defend itself "without destroying its neighbors' property".

Reagan changed too. With his Secretary of State, George Shultz, he made human rights a central part of negotiations, and in May 1988, standing in Red Square in Moscow, he declared that his phrase "evil empire" belonged to "another era".

This mattered because both leaders moved from confrontation to dialogue, which meant that by 1988 the arms race was being reversed and the Soviet Union had stopped treating the Cold War as an ideological struggle.

chunks.title: 1989–1991: the end of the Cold War
chunks.body:
The decisive change was Gorbachev's decision to let Eastern Europe go. His reforms legitimised calls for change, and he made clear, first in private and then in public, that the Soviet Union had abandoned the **Brezhnev Doctrine** of military intervention to save Communist regimes.

The regimes then fell, one after another, in 1989. In Poland, Round Table talks between the government and Solidarity began on 6 February; on 4 June Solidarity won a crushing election victory, and by 24 August Tadeusz Mazowiecki was the first non-Communist Prime Minister in Eastern Europe. Hungary opened its border with the West, giving East Germans an escape route. In East Germany, Erich Honecker was forced out in October, and on **9 November 1989** the Berlin Wall came down. Czechoslovakia had a non-Communist government by 5 December and elected the dissident playwright Václav Havel as President on 29 December. Only in Romania was there bloodshed: Ceauşescu was overthrown and executed on 25 December.

At Malta on 2 December 1989 President George Bush and Gorbachev, as one of Gorbachev's staff put it, "buried the Cold War at the bottom of the Mediterranean". Over the next year Gorbachev accepted a reunited Germany inside NATO, signed the Conventional Forces in Europe treaty, and, when Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, did not stand in Washington's way. James Baker called it "the world turned upside down". The Soviet Union itself did not survive. A failed hard-line coup in August 1991 "sealed the fate of the Soviet Union", and on 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time.

Who ended the Cold War? The Office of the Historian concludes that it ended "nearly entirely peacefully, and on U.S. terms". Judt is more cautious about Washington's role: "The US played a remarkably small part in the dramas of 1989, at least until after the fact." In his account the end came above all from Soviet weakness and Gorbachev's choices, with American pressure and Western support for dissidents in the background.

This mattered because the Cold War ended not with a victory in battle but with one side's decision to stop competing, which meant that it ended almost without bloodshed.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Peoples in Eastern Europe made the revolutions themselves.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Bush at first doubted Gorbachev's reforms would last.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Its collapse came after the Cold War had already ended in Europe.

options.text: In conclusion, the Soviet economy was bad and the Cold War ended.
In conclusion, money always decides wars.

The 'bleeding wound' speech of February 1986

segments.explanation: From the INF Treaty to Malta.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent were economic problems the main reason for the end of the Cold War between 1980 and 1991?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.scope: The end of the Cold War
decodeKey.judgement: Whether economics outweighed leadership, dissent and the arms race

modelPlan.thesis: Economic problems were a necessary condition of the end of the Cold War, because they made the arms race unsustainable for the USSR; but Gorbachev's decisions to negotiate and not to intervene were decisive.

arguments.claim: The military burden (named factor first).
Afghanistan as a drain and a humiliation.
Gorbachev's choices: INF and the Brezhnev Doctrine.
Dissent and popular revolution.

modelPlan.counter: Judt argues that bankruptcy alone would not have brought collapse; Brezhnev's stagnation might have lasted indefinitely.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Could the Cold War have ended without economic problems? Probably not, so they were necessary; but they were not sufficient.

segments.text: Economic problems were a necessary but not sufficient cause of the end of the Cold War.
At their peak 30–40 per cent of Soviet resources went to the military, four to five times the American share, and the Afghan war added a decade of losses.
This meant that the Soviet Union could not sustain a new arms race, so after 1985 reducing its foreign burdens became urgent.
However, Judt argues that 'bankruptcy alone would not have brought Communism to its knees'; it took Gorbachev's decisions to negotiate and to abandon the Brezhnev Doctrine.
Economic problems therefore explain why change was needed, while Gorbachev's choices explain why it happened.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Reagan's policies won the Cold War.” Discuss with reference to the period 1981 to 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: Whether US pressure or Soviet choices ended it

modelPlan.thesis: Reagan's rearmament raised the cost of the Cold War and his later diplomacy helped end it, but Soviet weakness and Gorbachev's choices were decisive; as Judt argues, the US played a small part in 1989.

arguments.claim: For: rearmament and SDI raised the cost.
For: the INF Treaty endorsed Reagan's 'zero option'.
Against: confrontation hardened the old Soviet leaders.
Against: Gorbachev's choices and the US's 'small part' in 1989.

modelPlan.counter: The Office of the Historian concludes the Cold War ended 'on U.S. terms'.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did Reagan's policies cause the Soviet decisions? Only partly: Gorbachev's priorities were domestic.

segments.text: Reagan's policies contributed to the end of the Cold War, but they did not win it alone.
Reagan raised defence spending by 6 per cent in 1985 and announced SDI, and the INF Treaty of 1987 endorsed his 'zero option'.
This meant that the arms race became more costly for the USSR, so a reforming leader had strong reasons to negotiate.
However, Judt argues that Reagan's hard line made the old leaders less willing to compromise, and that the US 'played a remarkably small part in the dramas of 1989'.
The claim is therefore exaggerated: Reagan raised the stakes, but Gorbachev's choices ended the Cold War.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the role of arms control agreements in ending the Cold War between 1985 and 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.scope: The end of the Cold War
decodeKey.judgement: Whether arms control caused the end or reflected it

modelPlan.thesis: Arms control played an important role, because the INF Treaty and later CFE and START reversed the military confrontation and built trust; but it was a means for Gorbachev's domestic aims and followed, rather than caused, his decision to end the rivalry.

arguments.claim: The INF Treaty of 1987.
CFE and START after Malta.
Gorbachev's domestic motives.
Limits: 1989 was decided by Soviet restraint and popular revolution.

modelPlan.counter: The revolutions of 1989 owed more to the Brezhnev Doctrine's abandonment than to any treaty.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did arms control cause the end or reflect it? Mainly reflect: it was the sign of Gorbachev's new thinking.

segments.text: Arms control was the visible sign that the Cold War was ending, rather than its main cause.
The INF Treaty of December 1987 eliminated an entire class of missiles, and after Malta in 1989 the CFE treaty and START followed.
This meant that the military confrontation was being reversed, so each side could trust the other's intentions.
However, Gorbachev pursued arms control to buy time for his domestic reforms, and the decisive events of 1989 came from his refusal to intervene.
Arms control's role was therefore important but secondary to Gorbachev's wider decision to end the rivalry.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons for, and the consequences of, the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan between 1985 and 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: Gorbachev withdrew from Afghanistan because the war was a costly humiliation that blocked his domestic priorities; its main consequence was that force could no longer be used to hold Eastern Europe.

arguments.claim: Reason: the 'bleeding wound' of a failed war.
Reason: Gorbachev's domestic priorities and new thinking.
Consequence: no further use of force in Eastern Europe.
Consequence: better relations with the West.

modelPlan.counter: Judt argues that the war alone would not have caused the Soviet collapse, so its consequences should not be exaggerated.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The rejection of force in Eastern Europe, which made 1989 possible.

segments.text: Gorbachev withdrew from Afghanistan mainly because the war blocked his priorities at home.
He called it the 'bleeding wound' in February 1986; withdrawal began in May 1988 and the last troops left on 15 February 1989.
This meant that the USSR accepted the limits of its military power, so, as Ligachev admitted, force in Eastern Europe was no longer possible.
However, Judt argues that the war, like the arms race, would not by itself have brought collapse.
The withdrawal's most important consequence was therefore the precedent it set for Eastern Europe in 1989.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons for the collapse of Communist regimes in Eastern Europe in 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The regimes collapsed because Gorbachev removed the guarantee of Soviet intervention, which allowed long-standing popular opposition, such as Solidarity, and economic failure to bring them down.

arguments.claim: The end of the Brezhnev Doctrine.
Solidarity and the Round Table in Poland.
Hungary's open border and the flight from the GDR.
The domino effect across the bloc.

modelPlan.counter: Romania shows that a regime willing to shoot could still resist for a time.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? Soviet restraint, without which, as 1953, 1956 and 1968 showed, protest would have been crushed.

segments.text: The regimes collapsed in 1989 mainly because Gorbachev removed the guarantee of Soviet intervention.
He made clear that the Brezhnev Doctrine was abandoned, and on 4 June Solidarity won the Polish elections while Hungary opened its border to the West.
This meant that the regimes could no longer rely on Soviet tanks, so when East Germans fled through Hungary and crowds marched, Honecker fell and the Wall came down.
However, popular movements made the revolutions: Solidarity had survived underground since 1981, and Havel's election showed the strength of dissent.
Soviet restraint was therefore the necessary condition, while popular opposition was the force that brought the regimes down.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the roles of the United States and the Soviet Union in ending the Cold War between 1985 and 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The roles of the two superpowers
decodeKey.scope: The end of the Cold War

modelPlan.thesis: Both superpowers chose negotiation after 1985, but the Soviet Union's role was decisive, because only Moscow could abandon the Brezhnev Doctrine, whereas the US, in Judt's words, played 'a remarkably small part' in 1989.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both negotiated arms control.
Similarity: both turned from hostility to dialogue.
Difference: Soviet restraint in Eastern Europe.
Difference: the US role in 1989.

modelPlan.counter: The Office of the Historian concludes the Cold War ended 'on U.S. terms', suggesting American pressure set the outcome.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Soviet restraint, because only Moscow could let Eastern Europe go.

segments.text: Both superpowers moved to negotiation after 1985, but the Soviet role was decisive.
Reagan and Gorbachev both signed the INF Treaty of 1987, whereas only Gorbachev could abandon the Brezhnev Doctrine and accept German unity within NATO.
This meant that the US could encourage change, but the USSR decided whether it would happen, so Soviet restraint allowed the revolutions of 1989.
However, the Office of the Historian argues the Cold War ended 'on U.S. terms', as German unity in NATO shows.
The decisive difference was therefore Soviet restraint, while American policy shaped the settlement that followed.
